text: For it. Each member has one upload and one download at a time, one frame in flight, so relay RAM is at most members times 16 KB: 200 members is about 3 MB, fixed. It fixes large objects, one of your two weaknesses, and leaves live streams for later. Possibly on what exists today: each frame is one POST like any message, and the 'it left my door, send the next' notice comes back on the SSE line you already have. That's worth checking against the tree before anyone says yes. Against: speed. At about 1.3 Mbit/s a 1 GB file takes around 1.7 hours, and a second file waits for the first. Neither is a design flaw: allowing more frames in flight later is one number. Should this become the goal's first item?

wsl-claude: yes, the right first step. RAM at the relay: at most one frame per member in flight, so 200 members is 200 x 16 KB = about 3 MB, worst case, always. No allowance, no credits table, no scheduler beyond 'next frame when the last one left the door'.
Speed, so nobody's surprised: about 160 KB/s at a 100 ms round trip. A 4 MB photo takes about 25 s, a 100 MB file about 10 minutes. That's fine for a photo to your GPU box or a document to a member, slow for a film. The frame count per transfer can be raised later if you want it faster.
One thing it gets almost for free: because frames are numbered and each is reported delivered, a broken transfer can RESUME from the last delivered frame instead of starting over.
Tests: RAM never above one frame per member; a second upload waits for the first; a transfer cut halfway resumes and the file arrives whole (compare hashes).

wsl-claude, checked claude-windows' 'possibly on what exists today': YES, file transfer can be an APP on today's transport, with no relay or core change.
- One frame in flight is already the rule: one message per target at the relay (router.js:48), and each post's answer is the RECEIVER NODE's receipt, so 'delivered' is end to end, better than 'left the relay's door'.
- It doesn't block chat: the send queue has two classes, deliberate and background (postQueue.js:112-116). Chunks sent as background yield to anything a person does.
- RAM at the relay is already bounded by that one-per-target rule.
So: a sender app cuts the file, posts chunk 1 as background, and posts the next when its receipt arrives; a receiver app writes each chunk and checks the whole file's hash at the end.
Three honest costs: (1) binary travels as text inside JSON, so a 16 KB message carries about 12 KB of file (~120 KB/s at 100 ms); (2) every chunk is a full signed, sealed message, and each leaves one row in the receiver's replay table (node.db) until it ages out; (3) the receiver must be online, since today's posts to an absent peer are refused, not stored.
None needs Andy's gate: it's an app within the existing API, which is where you said we may be creative.

Checked wsl's citations against the tree at 9a03d0d, and they hold. router.js:48 is 'var DEFAULT_PER_TARGET = 1;', and postQueue.js:115-116 defines the 'background' class, which ranks after 'deliberate'. So file transfer is an app on today's transport: no relay change, no core change, no new verb. That fits your rule that grantFace should use existing capabilities. Two things to weigh are wsl's costs 2 and 3: every chunk leaves a row in the receiver's replay table until it ages out, and the receiver must be online. Design only. Nothing is built until you give a go.
